title: Research Agents: Source Discovery, Citation Verification, and Synthesis
excerpt: Build research agents that verify source identity, map claims to evidence, preserve uncertainty, and produce citations readers can inspect and trust.
content:
A research agent should produce an inspectable argument, not merely a fluent answer with a bibliography. Its job is to discover relevant material, determine which version and scope apply, connect individual claims to evidence, and preserve uncertainty when the available record does not settle a question.

This guide proposes a research workflow with an evidence ledger and claim-level verification. The architecture and worked scenario are illustrative designs, not a tested product or a claim that automated checking establishes truth.

## Separate discovery, identity, support, and synthesis

A search result can be relevant without being reliable. A real paper can be irrelevant to the claim beside its citation. A supported sentence can still omit an important limitation. Treat these as different checks rather than one confidence score.

| Stage | Question | Inspectable output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discovery | What material might answer this question? | Candidate records and search queries |
| Identity | Is this the intended source and version? | Resolved identifier, title, publisher, version |
| Support | Does the accessible passage establish this claim? | Claim-to-passage relationship and qualification |
| Synthesis | What conclusion follows from the supported claims? | Answer with explicit assumptions and unresolved gaps |

The ALCE research benchmark evaluates generated answers along separate dimensions including correctness and citation quality. Its engineering relevance is the distinction: citations deserve their own assessment rather than being treated as a formatting feature. Its benchmark findings do not establish a reliability rate for an unrelated research agent. [ALCE paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14627).

For a production design, make the output of each stage available to the next as structured data. A later stage should not have to reconstruct source identity from a generated paragraph.

## Turn the question into a research contract

Before searching, capture the decision the answer must support. “Compare these systems” leaves too much implicit. “Determine whether either system satisfies our specified recovery requirement on the stated versions” identifies what evidence matters.

Record the relevant date, versions, environments, terminology, and exclusions. Distinguish a factual question from a recommendation. A recommendation additionally needs criteria and tradeoffs; retrieving a feature list does not supply the user's priorities.

Break the question into evidence obligations. A compatibility question might require the feature's introduction version, prerequisites, unsupported modes, and the behavior after interruption. Search separately for these obligations instead of repeatedly searching the original broad question.

This contract also defines a stopping rule. The agent can finish when required obligations have adequate evidence or are explicitly unresolved within the allotted budget. Finding an arbitrary number of sources is not a meaningful completion condition.

## Discover sources without counting duplicates as corroboration

Use broad discovery to learn terminology, then follow the trail toward material responsible for the claim: specifications, maintained documentation, original papers, release notes, or first-party incident accounts. Secondary explanations can identify useful questions, but should not quietly replace the underlying evidence.

Judge a source relative to the claim. Official documentation is appropriate for intended interface behavior. A provider's performance report describes its own reported experiment; it does not automatically establish expected performance on another workload. An independent measurement may answer a different question from a normative specification.

Track lineage. Three articles repeating one announcement provide three URLs and one underlying assertion. Group derivative reports with their origin when assessing corroboration. If two sources disagree, inspect their versions, conditions, and definitions before asking a model to choose the more persuasive prose.

Retrieved text remains untrusted input. A document may contain instructions addressed to the assistant, but those instructions do not acquire control-plane authority merely because the document is relevant. The broader enforcement design belongs in [prompt-injection defenses](/blog/prompt-injection-agent-defense).

## Verify source identity before using its content

For a scholarly reference, compare its identifier, title, authors, publication venue, and version with the cited item. Resolving a DOI verifies a particular identification path; it does not show that the paper supports the proposed sentence.

Crossref's REST API exposes deposited scholarly metadata, including bibliographic information and post-publication updates. Its documentation explains that records originate from members and trusted sources. Use such metadata to check identity and discover relevant updates, while recognizing that a metadata match is distinct from inspecting the research itself. [Crossref REST API documentation](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/rest-api/).

For a web document, record the requested URL, final URL after redirects, displayed title, relevant version, and retrieval time. A successful HTTP response can be a login screen, a generic home page, or an error message rendered with status 200. Confirm that the extracted content is the intended document.

If only an abstract is accessible, limit claims to what the abstract establishes. Do not describe an unseen method, limitation, or experiment as inspected. Mark unavailable full text as an evidence gap rather than generating a plausible continuation.

## Build an evidence ledger that survives drafting

In the proposed design, the ledger contains separate source snapshots, extracted passages, and claims. A compact relationship could look like this:

```json
{
  "claim_id": "claim_12",
  "claim": "Resumption requires a persistent upload session identifier.",
  "scope": {"product": "fictional Meridian SDK", "version": "4.2"},
  "source_snapshot": "source_17@revision_3",
  "locator": "Uploads / Recovery / paragraph 2",
  "relationship": "supports_with_conditions",
  "conditions": ["session has not expired"],
  "verification": "passage_review_required"
}
```

Every identifier and product in this example is fictional. The important design choice is the separation between a proposed claim, its scope, the exact evidence location, and the verification state.

W3C's PROV overview describes provenance through the entities, activities, and agents involved in producing information. That vocabulary is useful for distinguishing a retrieved document from an extraction activity and a later synthesis artifact. Adopting a provenance representation does not certify the source's truth. [W3C PROV overview](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-overview/).

Store bounded passages with surrounding context and an integrity reference, subject to access rights and retention policy. Keep enough context to preserve exceptions, headings, and table labels. A content hash can reveal that retained bytes changed; it cannot establish that those bytes were accurate or authoritative.

## Verify claims at the smallest useful unit

A sentence may combine several propositions: a feature exists, it arrived in a particular version, it works across regions, and it improves recovery time. One citation might support only the first. Split the sentence or attach evidence to each proposition.

FActScore evaluates factual precision by decomposing generated text into atomic facts and checking support against a knowledge source. Its original study concerns particular generated text and evaluation settings; the transferable idea here is to inspect smaller assertions instead of assigning one factuality judgment to an entire answer. [FActScore paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14251).

Use at least four verification outcomes: supported, contradicted, insufficient evidence, and inaccessible evidence. Keep direct observations separate from derived conclusions. If a recommendation combines documented features with an assumed workload, state the assumption and show the reasoning rather than presenting the recommendation as a quotation from the sources.

An automated verifier can propose these labels, but its evidence and rationale should remain reviewable. For consequential decisions, a second model's agreement is not a substitute for checking the actual passage and applicable conditions.

## Walk through a hypothetical version conflict

Assume a user asks whether fictional Meridian SDK 4.2 can resume interrupted uploads after a worker restart. The research contract requires evidence about client support, persisted identifiers, session expiry, and server-side compatibility.

The agent finds a 4.1 guide describing restart behavior, a 4.2 release note adding a recovery helper, and a tutorial claiming that every upload resumes automatically. The tutorial links back to the release note, so it is not independent confirmation.

The ledger records the guide as older-version evidence and the release note as evidence for a newly introduced helper. Neither automatically supports persistence across a process restart. The agent searches specifically for session persistence and expiry, rather than promoting the tutorial's broad claim into the answer.

Suppose the relevant documentation says that recovery requires storing the session identifier and that sessions can expire. The final answer should state those conditions and identify any unverified server configuration. If persistence documentation remains unavailable, the answer should remain conditional instead of silently treating the helper's existence as proof of end-to-end recovery.

## Evaluate the research process, not only the prose

Create cases with misleading snippets, redirected URLs, duplicate reporting, outdated versions, inaccessible full text, and citations that support only half a sentence. Include questions whose correct outcome is an explicit evidence gap.

Inspect source identity, claim support, citation coverage, important omissions, and the correctness of derived conclusions separately. A short answer can achieve excellent support coverage by omitting the difficult part of the user's question, so also evaluate whether the research contract was fulfilled.

Measure acquisition and verification cost alongside accepted answer quality. If a run spends its budget reopening equivalent sources, improve its discovery state and stopping conditions. For evidence selection under a limited context window, see [RAG reranking and context selection](/blog/rag-reranking-context-selection).

## Frequently asked questions

### Does a working citation link prove the claim is correct?

No. It establishes that a destination is reachable. The destination may be the wrong version, contain a qualified statement, or fail to support the claim altogether. Identity and support require separate checks.

### Should the agent quote every supporting passage?

No. Retain suitable evidence internally and cite concise, relevant material in the answer. Excessive quotation adds reading burden and can exceed reuse permissions. A precise paraphrase still needs support and attribution.

### When should a research agent stop searching?

Stop when the required evidence obligations are satisfied or the remaining gaps are explicitly reported within the task's resource limits. More sources are useful when they resolve uncertainty, not simply when they enlarge the bibliography.
